query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Combining in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) with thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) during oxidation tests will enable real-time observation of both phase transformations and mass changes, thereby clarifying the dynamic relationship between oxide scale growth and phase stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized metal or high-entropy alloy sample with an initially single-phase microstructure (e.g., FCC or BCC) prior to high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Subject the material to in situ HTXRD in parallel with TGA under oxidizing conditions, monitoring phase evolution by diffraction patterns while simultaneously measuring mass changes due to oxidation.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–900 °C or higher) in controlled oxidizing environments for time intervals relevant to the intended high-temperature application.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time correlation between TGA mass data and in situ diffraction peak intensities and/or shifts to identify evolving oxide layers and new phases.
generation.mechanism: Continuous phase mapping from HTXRD, along with oxidation rate tracking from TGA, illuminates how emergent oxide phases, elemental diffusion, and structural changes influence—and are influenced by—ongoing oxidation reactions under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Time-resolved TGA–HTXRD data will reveal a strong correlation between the rate of mass gain and the appearance or transformation of oxide phases, confirming that the combined technique can precisely link oxidation kinetics to phase evolution in real time.
generation.baseline: Conventional ex situ oxidation and post-exposure XRD analyses only capture final or intermittent states, making it difficult to track transient phase transformations and their link to oxidation kinetics.
generation.boundary: Measurements require specialized X-ray instrumentation capable of high-temperature in situ operation; results may vary depending on sample geometry, atmosphere control, and detection limits for minor phases.
generation.uncertainty: While combined in situ HTXRD-TGA techniques offer improved clarity into phase evolution, external variables like oxygen partial pressure, temperature gradients, and geometric factors can introduce measurement errors or data interpretation challenges.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct two parallel oxidation studies on identical alloy specimens. Monitor one set continuously in situ with simultaneous HTXRD and TGA. Analyze the other set solely by standard ex situ methods (e.g., weigh samples and collect XRD spectra at fixed time intervals). Compare recorded phase evolution timelines, oxidation rates, and final state microstructures to validate whether the in situ approach accurately captures all salient transformation events.
measurements: Time-resolved diffraction data (peak positions and intensities) from HTXRD.
Real-time mass gain measurements from TGA.
Post-mortem microstructural characterization using SEM/EDS and ex situ XRD.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If in situ HTXRD data do not align with TGA mass change profiles, or if ex situ analyses reveal missed phases and discrepancies in oxidation product formation, the hypothesis—that combined in situ TGA-HTXRD can reliably capture real-time phase evolution—will be disproven.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. decision.trend: Earlier work on high-temperature oxidation in HEAs has typically involved prolonged furnace exposures at elevated temperatures in air (600–900 °C) or controlled atmospheres, with periodic or final mass measurements to evaluate oxidation kinetics. Phase identification and scale characterization often relied on ex situ XRD or cross-sectional microscopy after the tests. These studies successfully revealed oxidation rates, scale morphologies, and phase evolution, but real-time insights into how phases evolve and react during heating and exposure remain elusive. More precise, continuous methods to capture evolving phase equilibria in situ are lacking.
decision.unsolved: Although weight-gain measurements and post-exposure analyses reveal total oxidation rates and final phase constitutions, they do not clarify the dynamics of oxide growth and transformations in real time. Obtaining time-resolved phase evolution data to correlate oxidation kinetics with specific microstructural or phase changes remains a challenge.
decision.lever: Combine in situ high-temperature XRD with thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to track real-time phase transformations and mass changes during oxidation up to the target temperature range (≥800 °C); accompany with postmortem microstructural characterization to confirm oxide scale morphology and composition
decision.why: This approach provides continuous, in situ monitoring of both oxidation kinetics (via TGA) and phase evolution (via high-temperature XRD), resolving the key challenge of correlating oxide growth stages and phase changes throughout the oxidation process. It builds directly on the furnace-based oxidation tests and post-analysis from prior studies, adding powerful real-time insight into underlying mechanisms by capturing transformations as they occur.
